title: Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL
goal: By the end, you can name the four ideas a distributed SQL database is built from, explain three ways such a database gives its transactions an order that matches real time (one server that hands out timestamps, Spanner's clock that waits out its own error, CockroachDB's readers that restart), and say what each costs and which isolation it gives.
opening:
Picture paying a friend back. You send 20.00 from your banking app, it says Sent, and you text them: done. They open their app a second later, and the money isn't there. Then it appears. For a moment, their app showed a world where you hadn't paid.

Now spread the bank's database over many machines, each with its own clock. The natural way to order changes is by time. Stamp each one with the clock of the machine that made it, and let a report read everything stamped before it began. Phone clocks agree to the second, so this feels safe. But server clocks disagree by milliseconds, and a payment stamped by a fast clock can look newer than a report that started after it.

Coordination services: ZooKeeper, etcd and KRaft numbered every change on one small group of servers. In this lesson, we'll build a SQL database from many Raft groups, then compare three ways to stamp its transactions so a later report always sees an earlier payment. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Two servers' clocks may differ by up to 20 ms. A payment commits on server W, stamped with W's clock reading, and the customer is told "paid". One millisecond later, a report on server R reads the account as of R's clock reading: it sees every change stamped at or before that time. What can the report see?
options: Always the payment: it committed before the report started
Possibly the old balance: if R's clock is behind W's, the report's time can be earlier than the payment's stamp
Half of the payment, because the two servers disagree
Nothing: the read fails with a clock error
warmup.why: A report like this, called a snapshot read, returns what was committed at or below its timestamp. If W's clock is ahead, the payment's stamp can be up to 20 ms above R's reading, even though the payment really happened first, so the report misses it. Stamping both rows of the payment with one timestamp keeps the report from seeing half of it, which rules out the third option; it doesn't make the stamps agree with real time. That gap is what this lesson's designs close, each at a different price.

sections.h: One transfer, two machines: the four layers of a distributed SQL database
sections.body:
Let's move 100.00 from a customer's account, `A-1001`, to a shop's account, `M-2001`. In a big payments app, the two rows live on different machines. The database must still make the transfer one transaction: a group of changes that happen all together or not at all, with no half-done state anyone can see. And the app shouldn't need special code for it. A database that does this for SQL, across many machines, is called distributed SQL. Spanner (Google's), CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB and Aurora DSQL (Amazon's) are examples, and FoundationDB does it for a simpler store of keys and values. Each is built from four ideas that earlier tracks taught, and the figure stacks them.

The first is splitting by key ranges, from the Partitioning track. The table's keys are cut into ranges, slices such as "everything below M", and each range lives on a few machines. CockroachDB splits a range when it grows past 512 MiB (about half a gigabyte), so `A-1001` can sit in one range and `M-2001` in the next.

The second is a consensus group per range, from Consensus with Raft. Each range is copied to three or five servers by its own Raft group (Paxos, in Spanner), with its own leader. A range survives the loss of a server, and its leader puts that range's writes in one order. A cluster runs thousands of these small groups, so the leaders spread over every machine.

The third is two-phase commit across ranges, from Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA. The transfer first writes provisional values, called **intents**, into both ranges. Then one record, the transaction record, says commit or abort. That lesson's worst case was a coordinator, the server running the commit, that dies and leaves everyone else waiting, still holding locks. Here that case goes away, because the transaction record and every intent are themselves writes to Raft groups. They survive the loss of any one machine, and another server can finish the commit.

The fourth is timestamps, from the Faults, time and truth track. Each range keeps old versions of its rows (MVCC, multi-version concurrency control, from the Transactions track), so a reader can take a snapshot: everything committed at or below timestamp T. That works only if every commit carries a timestamp, and both rows of one transfer carry the same one. On one machine, a counter does it.

Across a thousand machines, two questions are left. Who hands out the timestamps? And does a higher timestamp mean later in real time? Those questions separate the designs in this lesson. They also decide whether the strongest promise from Consistency models: what a read may return holds. That promise, strict serializability, says transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, in the order they really happened.

The Try it shows the first three layers in a real CockroachDB 26.3, and the transfer's two rows committed at one timestamp. Next, we'll try the simplest way to hand out timestamps.

try.title: Two ranges, one commit timestamp
steps: Start CockroachDB 26.3 on one node (about 1 GB of memory), and a helper, `sql`, that runs one statement: `docker run -d --name sfz-crdb -m 1g cockroachdb/cockroach:v26.3.5 start-single-node --insecure --cache=128MiB --max-sql-memory=128MiB`, then `sql() { docker exec -i sfz-crdb ./cockroach sql --insecure -e "$1"; }`.
Create the accounts, split the table into two ranges at 'M', and list the ranges with their leaseholder (the copy that serves reads and leads writes for that range) and their replicas (its copies).

Wait ten seconds. Then run the transfer as one transaction, and read each row with the hidden column `crdb_internal_mvcc_timestamp`, the timestamp its version was committed at. Predict first: will the two rows, in two ranges, show the same timestamp?
Read the table as it was ten seconds ago with `AS OF SYSTEM TIME`, then stop: `docker rm -f sfz-crdb`.

code.title: in any terminal
code.src:
sql "CREATE TABLE accounts (id STRING PRIMARY KEY, balance INT NOT NULL);"
sql "INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('A-1001', 500), ('M-2001', 0);"
sql "ALTER TABLE accounts SPLIT AT VALUES ('M');"
sql "SELECT start_key, end_key, range_id, lease_holder, replicas FROM [SHOW RANGES FROM TABLE accounts WITH DETAILS];"
sleep 10
sql "BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A-1001'; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 'M-2001'; COMMIT;"
sql "SELECT id, balance, crdb_internal_mvcc_timestamp FROM accounts;"
sql "SELECT id, balance FROM accounts AS OF SYSTEM TIME '-10s';"

try.expect:
```text
      start_key      |   end_key    | range_id | lease_holder | replicas
---------------------+--------------+----------+--------------+-----------
  <before:/Table/84> | …/1/"M"      |       87 |            1 | {1}
  …/1/"M"            | <after:/Max> |       88 |            1 | {1}

    id   | balance |  crdb_internal_mvcc_timestamp
---------+---------+---------------------------------
  A-1001 |     400 | 1794118781781941837.0000000000
  M-2001 |     100 | 1794118781781941837.0000000000

    id   | balance
---------+----------
  A-1001 |     500
  M-2001 |       0
```

The split made two ranges, 87 and 88, each with a leaseholder and a set of replicas, here only node 1. Both rows of the transfer carry the same commit timestamp, although they live in different ranges: two-phase commit stamped them together. The timestamp is a hybrid logical clock value, which the fourth section explains: nanoseconds of wall-clock time before the dot, and a counter after it. The `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` read is a snapshot from before the transfer, served from the old versions. Range ids and timestamps differ on your machine. Output trimmed: the statements' own `CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT` and `COMMIT` lines.

sections.h: The simplest answer: one server hands out every timestamp
sections.body:
Picture bank branches in different towns, each stamping deposit slips with its own wall clock. The simplest fix is a head office that gives out every slip number by phone: the numbers are always in order, and every branch waits on the line. In a database, that head office is a **timestamp oracle**, one server that hands out every timestamp. Google's Percolator (2010) added transactions to its Bigtable database this way. One machine gave out timestamps that only went up, about 2 million a second, by handing them out in batches.

TiDB, a distributed SQL database, copies Percolator. Its Placement Driver, a small cluster that also tracks where every range lives, hands out each timestamp. A timestamp is milliseconds of clock time plus a counter. The counter moves on when two timestamps are needed in the same millisecond, or when the clock steps backwards, so a timestamp never repeats and never goes down. A transaction asks the oracle for a start timestamp and reads the snapshot at it. It then locks and writes its rows across ranges with two-phase commit, over the Raft groups of TiKV, TiDB's storage layer. Finally it asks the oracle again, for a commit timestamp.

Because one server issues every number, the numbers follow real time. If transfer T1 commits before audit T2 starts, T2's start timestamp is higher than T1's commit timestamp, and T2's snapshot includes T1. Designing Data-Intensive Applications calls this a linearizable ID generator: the single copy of Linearizability: one copy, one timeline, in another form. The payment from the warm-up can't be missed.

FoundationDB does the same with a sequencer that hands out commit versions, about a million a second. It adds optimistic concurrency: transactions run without locks, and clashes are checked at the end. A transaction reads at a read version and holds its writes back. At commit, servers called resolvers check whether anything it read was overwritten since its read version, and abort it if so. The result is strict serializability without locks. The resolvers keep only five seconds of history, so a transaction that runs longer than that is rejected.

The price is the oracle itself. Every transaction makes one or two round trips to it before it can commit, and it's one leader, copied so that a standby can take over, but not spread out. In one region, a group of nearby data centres, that adds a fraction of a millisecond. With servers in two regions, a transaction far from the oracle pays a round trip of about 70 ms for each timestamp. Spanner set out to remove the oracle altogether.

refs.title: Zhou et al.: FoundationDB, a distributed unbundled transactional key value store (SIGMOD 2021)
Peng and Dabek: Large-scale incremental processing using distributed transactions and notifications (Percolator, OSDI 2010)

sections.h: Spanner: know the clock's error, and wait it out
sections.body:
Spanner (Google, 2012) has no oracle. Each server stamps commits from its own clock. The Faults, time and truth track showed why that's dangerous: clocks disagree, and a clock reading says nothing about its own error. Spanner's fix is a clock that reports its error. **TrueTime** returns an interval, `TT.now() = [earliest, latest]`, and guarantees that the true time is inside it. GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every data centre keep the interval narrow. In the 2012 paper, ε (epsilon), half the interval's width, grew from about 1 to 7 ms between checks against the time servers every 30 seconds. So it was about 4 ms most of the time, with spikes when a time server or the network misbehaved. Google hasn't published newer figures.

A transaction that writes takes locks and runs two-phase commit across the Paxos groups of the ranges it touched. Its coordinator picks a commit timestamp no lower than `TT.now().latest`, the top of the interval. Then comes the rule that gives the design its name, **commit wait**: the coordinator releases no locks and tells no one about the commit until `TT.now().earliest` has passed the timestamp. The timestamp was picked at the top of an interval, and the wait ends when the bottom reaches it, so the wait is about 2ε. In the branch picture, each clerk's clock is certified to within a few seconds, and the clerk holds every slip until that many seconds have passed.

When the client hears "committed", the commit timestamp is in the past on every clock. Any transaction that starts afterwards reads at `TT.now().latest`, which is at or above the true time. So its timestamp is higher, and its snapshot includes the commit. Spanner calls this external consistency; Consistency models: what a read may return called it strict serializability.

The wait would hurt if it came on top of everything else, so Spanner runs it while Paxos copies the commit record. The 2012 paper measured commit wait at about 5 ms, next to about 9 ms of Paxos time, and a mean write time of about 14 ms. Up-to-date reads pay a little too. A read at `TT.now().latest` may have to wait until its copies are sure no transaction can still commit below that timestamp. The lab models this as a read that waits on an intent.

Spanner's default stays serializable. It now also offers REPEATABLE READ, which is snapshot isolation: each transaction reads one snapshot, and only clashing writes are checked. That allows write skew, from the Transactions track: two transactions read the same rows, write different ones, and together break a rule that neither broke alone. Some programs accept it, because reads no longer wait behind writes.

The stepper and the Try it use two servers. `settle` pays batch 1 of the nightly payout, and `audit-0` runs an audit, a report that checks the books. Next, we'll see how CockroachDB gets the same order without special clocks.

frames.say: The `settle` server's clock reads 10 ms when the true time is 0: it's 10 ms fast, and it doesn't know that. It does know its error bound, ε = 10 ms, so TrueTime reports the interval **[0, 20]**: the true time is somewhere in there. Spanner's rule picks the commit timestamp at the top, **s = 20**, so s can't be earlier than the moment it was chosen.

frames.say: One millisecond later, an audit starts on a server whose clock is 10 ms slow. Its TrueTime says [1, 21], and an up-to-date read uses the top, **21**. The commit was announced only once s = 20 had passed, so any read that starts afterwards picks a timestamp above 20. **The audit sees batch 1**: external consistency, which is strict serializability.

frames.say: Now the same two servers **trust their clocks**. `settle` commits at what its clock read when it started, s = 10, and answers at 8 ms. At 9 ms the audit reads at what its clock says, -1. The batch was paid before the audit began, and the audit doesn't see it: a stale read, caused only by 20 ms of disagreement between two clocks. The demo's `trust` scenario prints this run.

stepper.intro: Two servers: `settle`, whose clock runs 10 ms fast, pays batch 1; `audit-0`, whose clock runs 10 ms slow, checks the books. Use Next and Back, or the arrow keys.

try.title: Watch commit wait, then trust the clocks
steps: `UncertaintyDemo.kt` runs one payout transaction across two ranges on a server whose clock is 10 ms fast. Then it starts one audit, 1 ms after the client was told, on a server whose clock is 10 ms slow. No Docker needed.
Run `commitwait`, and find when the client is told and the timestamp the audit reads at.
Predict what the audit sees when the same servers trust their clocks, then run `trust`. Try `commitwait 3` too: does a 3 ms bound add any wait to an 8 ms commit?
try.expect:
```text
COMMIT_WAIT, clocks within 10 ms of true time: settle runs 10 ms ahead, audit-0 10 ms behind
t=    0  settle   batch 1: commit timestamp 20 (its clock reads 10)
t=    4  settle   intents for batch 1 written to payouts and ledger at 20
t=    8  settle   commit record replicated: batch 1 is decided
t=   20  settle   commit wait over: TrueTime earliest is now 20, so 20 has surely passed
t=   20  settle   client told: batch 1 is paid (20 ms)
t=   21  audit-0  audit starts: read timestamp 21 (clock 11)
t=   23  audit-0  reads payouts = 1, ledger = 1
fresh: the audit sees batch 1 (0 restart(s), waited 0 ms)
```

```text
TRUST_CLOCK, clocks within 10 ms of true time: settle runs 10 ms ahead, audit-0 10 ms behind
t=    0  settle   batch 1: commit timestamp 10 (its clock reads 10)
t=    4  settle   intents for batch 1 written to payouts and ledger at 10
t=    8  settle   commit record replicated: batch 1 is decided
t=    8  settle   client told: batch 1 is paid (8 ms)
t=    9  audit-0  audit starts: read timestamp -1 (clock -1)
t=   11  audit-0  reads payouts = 0, ledger = 0
STALE: batch 1 was acknowledged before this audit began, and the audit missed it
```

With commit wait, the transaction was decided at 8 ms but announced at 20 ms, 2ε after it picked s = 20, and the audit's timestamp, 21, came out above it. Trusting the clocks answered 12 ms sooner, and the audit missed a batch that was already paid, though it still saw both ranges agree. With `commitwait 3`, 2ε is 6 ms, less than the 8 ms the commit needs anyway, so the client is told at 8 ms: the wait hides entirely behind the copying.

aside.title: Why not put a perfect clock in every server?
aside.body: Because no clock is perfect, and the error is what costs you, not the clock. Spanner's GPS and atomic clocks bring ε down to a few milliseconds, never to zero, so Spanner still waits. Cloud clocks keep improving: AWS's Time Sync Service reports error bounds under 40 µs (millionths of a second) through its Nitro hardware clock. As the bound shrinks, commit wait shrinks toward nothing, and so does every other design's clock cost.

sections.h: CockroachDB: no special clocks, so the reader handles the doubt
sections.body:
CockroachDB runs on ordinary servers, which it calls nodes, whose clocks are set over the network by NTP, the time-setting protocol from the Faults, time and truth track. Their error can reach hundreds of milliseconds, so a 2ε commit wait on every write would be far too slow. CockroachDB takes two ideas instead.

The first is a **hybrid logical clock** (HLC), from Ordering without a shared clock: logical clocks and IDs. A node's timestamp is its wall-clock time plus a counter, and a node that receives a higher timestamp in a message moves its own clock up to it. So when one event causes another, the second always gets the higher timestamp, even between nodes whose clocks disagree. The first Try it showed one: wall-clock nanoseconds, a dot, then the counter.

The second is a promised bound on how far clocks may disagree, the **max offset**: 500 ms by default, and 250 ms suggested for new clusters spread over several regions. The bound is enforced. A node whose clock is off from at least half of the other nodes by 80% of the max offset shuts itself down, rather than serve wrong answers.

Writers don't wait at all. A read at timestamp T knows that any value with a timestamp above T + max offset was written after it began, whatever the clocks say. A value between T and T + max offset is in the read's **uncertainty interval**: it may have committed before the read started, on a node whose clock runs ahead. The read can't skip it, so it moves its own timestamp up past that value. If its earlier reads still hold at the new timestamp, it carries on. Otherwise the transaction restarts, with an error called `ReadWithinUncertaintyIntervalError`. The top of the interval doesn't move with the timestamp, so the restarts must end. The cost lands only on reads of keys written within the last max offset, instead of on every write.

In the branch picture, clerks stamp slips at once, and an auditor who finds a slip stamped right after the audit began starts over, counting it in. The picture breaks on scale: clerks would hold slips or recount for seconds, while servers do it for milliseconds, thousands of times a second. That's why a few milliseconds of clock error become a cost you can measure.

Writes are intents with a transaction record, as in the first section. With **parallel commits**, the record is set to STAGING while the intents are still being copied. The transaction counts as committed once every intent has reached consensus, so a commit takes one round of consensus instead of two, and the intents are tidied up afterwards.

The guarantee is serializable by default, but not strictly. CockroachDB's documentation says that clocks off by more than the max offset can break real-time order, even on one key, between transactions where one depends on the other. YugabyteDB works the same way, with hybrid time and a 500 ms default bound.

**The bound on the clock's error, not the clock's reading, sets the price. Know your bound.** Next, we'll meet a design that takes no locks during a transaction, and checks once at the end.

try.title: Restart above a value you can't place
steps: Run the `restart` scenario: the same two servers, transaction and audit as the last Try it, under CockroachDB's rules. The writer commits at its clock, and the reader's window reaches 2ε above its own clock.
Find the read timestamp, the top of its window, and the timestamp it restarts at. How long did the client wait for its commit this time, and how long the audit?
Run `restart 1`: with clocks within 1 ms, is the batch inside the window?
try.expect:
```text
RESTART, clocks within 10 ms of true time: settle runs 10 ms ahead, audit-0 10 ms behind
t=    0  settle   batch 1: commit timestamp 10 (its clock reads 10)
t=    4  settle   intents for batch 1 written to payouts and ledger at 10
t=    8  settle   commit record replicated: batch 1 is decided
t=    8  settle   client told: batch 1 is paid (8 ms)
t=    9  audit-0  audit starts: read timestamp -1 (clock -1), uncertain up to 19
t=   11  audit-0  finds a version it can't place: restarts at 10
t=   13  audit-0  reads payouts = 1, ledger = 1
fresh: the audit sees batch 1 (1 restart(s), waited 0 ms)
```

The writer answered at 8 ms, as fast as trusting the clocks. The audit read at -1, but its window reached 19 (2ε above its clock, the most two clocks can disagree), and the batch's timestamp, 10, fell inside it. So it restarted at 10 and saw the batch: one extra round trip, 4 ms in all instead of 2. With `restart 1`, the window is 2 ms wide and the clocks barely disagree, so the batch's timestamp is already below the read timestamp: no restart.

sections.h: Aurora DSQL checks once at commit, and what each design costs
sections.body:
Aurora DSQL (Amazon Web Services, generally available since May 2025) makes a different trade: **optimistic concurrency at snapshot isolation only**. A transaction reads at its start time from storage that keeps old versions, with no locks and no coordination. (Storage first waits until it has applied every commit at or below that time.) Writes stay in the query processor, the part that runs your SQL, until COMMIT. Then a component called an adjudicator checks whether another transaction wrote the same keys since this one started. If one did, the later one fails with error code SQLSTATE 40001 (and DSQL's own code OC000), and the app retries. The commit is final once DSQL's journal, its replicated log, stores it.

That's one coordination step per transaction, at commit, and no deadlocks (two transactions each waiting for a lock the other holds), since nothing waits on a lock. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` counts as a write when the adjudicator checks.

The limits come with the design. Snapshot isolation is PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ, so write skew is possible: two transactions that each read two fee limits and lower a different one can both commit. A transaction may change at most 3,000 rows and 10 MiB, and may run at most 5 minutes. And a hot key, such as a shop's balance row that every payment updates, turns into a retry loop, because every writer but one fails at commit.

So "distributed SQL" doesn't mean "serializable". Spanner and CockroachDB default to serializable and now offer weaker levels. TiDB and YugabyteDB default to snapshot isolation, and Aurora DSQL offers nothing else. Read the isolation level in the documentation, not on the product page.

Here is where each design charges for the same transfer, with a consensus round inside one region of about 1 to 2 ms:

| System | Commit timestamp from | A write pays | A read pays | Default isolation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TiDB | an oracle (the Placement Driver) | two oracle trips, two-phase commit over Raft | one oracle trip | snapshot (REPEATABLE READ), with locks |
| FoundationDB | a sequencer | a version, a resolver check | a read version | strict serializable (optimistic) |
| Spanner | TrueTime | commit wait of about 2ε, overlapped with Paxos | may wait on recent writes | serializable (external consistency) |
| CockroachDB | hybrid clock, max offset | one consensus round (parallel commits) | a restart if a value is uncertain | serializable |
| Aurora DSQL | adjudicators at commit | one adjudication, one journal write | nothing extra | snapshot only |

All of them pay a consensus round per write and some coordination per transaction, where one PostgreSQL server pays a single flush to disk. You buy that for data that outgrows one machine, or for a database that keeps working when a whole region is lost. The Try it measures the clock part on its own.

Find where trusting the clocks starts to give stale audits, and where commit wait stops hiding behind the 8 ms commit.

Restarts cost writes nothing, and add about one round trip to the audits that meet a fresh value. Here that's most audits, because every auditor reads the one key the job rewrites every 10 to 20 ms. That's the worst case; a real table spreads its reads over many keys. Trusting the clocks is the fastest and, from ε = 5 ms up, wrong more often than you'd ever ship. The run is seeded, so these numbers are exact.

compare.title: One transfer's commit path in Spanner and in CockroachDB

a.label: Spanner
a.title: TrueTime and commit wait
a.src:
1  lock A-1001 and M-2001 (two-phase locking)
2  prepare in both Paxos groups
3  s = TT.now().latest
4  replicate the commit record   (Paxos)
5  wait until TT.now().earliest > s
   (about 2 x epsilon, overlapped with 4)
6  release locks, tell the client

readers: read at TT.now().latest,
         may wait for safe time

b.label: CockroachDB
b.title: hybrid clock and uncertainty
b.src:
1  ts = HLC.now() at the gateway node
2  write intents in both Raft groups
   and set the record to STAGING
   (parallel commits: one round)
3  tell the client once all are replicated
4  resolve the intents afterwards

readers: value in (T, T + max offset]?
         move T above it, refresh
         or restart

compare.note: Both make a transaction's timestamp agree with real time, and both depend on a bound on clock error. Spanner makes every writer wait out its bound, which is small thanks to special hardware, so readers never doubt a timestamp. CockroachDB's bound is large (500 ms by default), because it runs on ordinary clocks. Making writers wait that long would be too slow, so it lets readers find the doubtful values, and pay only when they meet one. Which costs less depends on the clock, and on how often reads touch freshly written keys.

worked.title: Work out the clock's cost for three kinds of clock

steps.say: Write the two costs as formulas. If every clock is within ε of the true time, two clocks can differ by up to 2ε. Commit wait adds whatever part of the wait the copying doesn't hide. An uncertainty window catches values written up to 2ε after a read's clock.
steps.code:
commitWait(eps, replicationMs) = max(0, 2 * eps - replicationMs)
windowMs(eps)                  = 2 * eps   // CockroachDB: --max-offset

steps.say: AWS's Time Sync Service, with its Nitro hardware clock, reports error bounds under 40 µs (millionths of a second). The wait vanishes behind a 1 ms consensus round, and the window is tiny.
steps.code:
eps = 0.04 ms, replication 1 ms
commit wait  = max(0, 0.08 - 1) = 0 ms
window       = 0.08 ms

steps.say: Spanner's 2012 numbers: ε about 4 ms (peaks near 7), Paxos about 9 ms. The formula says the wait could hide entirely. Yet the paper's one-copy test took 14.4 ms per write with commit wait and 9.4 ms without, about 5 ms more. Overlap hides part of the wait, not all of it, so treat the formula as a lower bound.
steps.code:
eps = 4 ms (peaks 7), replication about 9 ms
formula: max(0, 8 - 9)  = 0 ms
measured: 14.4 - 9.4    = about 5 ms

steps.say: Clocks set over the public internet by NTP, with tens of ms of error. Commit wait would add most of a 100 ms window to every write, so this is CockroachDB's territory: no wait, and reads of keys written in the last few hundred ms may restart.
steps.code:
eps = 50 ms, replication 2 ms
commit wait  = max(0, 100 - 2) = 98 ms per write
window       = 100 ms (CockroachDB default max offset: 500 ms)

steps.say: The lesson in code: the bound, not the clock reading, sets the price. Here's a small Kotlin check, with the same numbers, that you could run when a server starts.

lab.title: Commit timestamps on clocks that disagree
steps: Read `Clocks.kt`: a clock with an offset it doesn't know about, and a TrueTime interval around it. Then read the half of `Transactions.kt` that's written for you. `settle` runs the two-range transaction, and `checkedAudit` marks an audit stale, or fractured (it saw one range's half of a transfer and not the other's). Processes are plain Kotlin that call `sim.sleep`, and a pretend clock makes ten seconds of traffic run in milliseconds. Run the tests once: all 14 fail.

Write `Range.read` in `Mvcc.kt`. An intent at or below the window's top blocks the read, a committed version inside the window is uncertain, and otherwise it returns the snapshot value. The three `RangeTest` tests pass.
Write `commitTimestamp` and `commitWait`: either the clock, or TrueTime's latest followed by a wait until TrueTime's earliest reaches the timestamp. The commit-wait test passes with exactly 20 ms.

Write `audit`. Pick the read timestamp and window for the policy, then loop: one round trip, read both ranges, wait 1 ms on an intent, restart above an uncertain value. The remaining tests pass, including a property test over hundreds of seeds and bounds: commit wait and restarts never give a stale or fractured audit.
hints: In `Range.read`, check intents before uncertainty. An intent you skip could commit at a timestamp below yours a moment later, and a reader that ignores it can see one range's half of a transfer and not the other's.
For RESTART the window is `readTs + 2 * epsilonMs`, because the writer's clock may be ε ahead of the true time while yours is ε behind.
When you restart, move `readTs` up to the uncertain timestamp, but leave the window's top where it was. A window that moved with the read could find a new uncertain value on every attempt.
A wait on an intent sleeps 1 ms with no new round trip; a restart costs `rttMs`. The exact-time tests depend on that difference.

drill.title: Write the read rule from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write `read(key, readTs, limit)` for one range that keeps old versions. Block on an intent at or below the limit. Report the highest committed timestamp in (readTs, limit] as uncertain. Otherwise, return the newest committed version at or below readTs.

recap: A distributed SQL database stacks four earlier ideas: key ranges on many machines, a Raft or Paxos group per range, two-phase commit across ranges with intents and a replicated transaction record, and versioned rows read at a commit timestamp.
The timestamps decide the guarantee. A timestamp oracle (Percolator, TiDB's Placement Driver, FoundationDB's sequencer) follows real time, but every transaction pays a round trip to one leader.

Spanner's TrueTime reports [earliest, latest]. A transaction commits at latest and waits about 2ε, until earliest passes it, overlapped with Paxos. That buys external consistency, which is strict serializability.

CockroachDB uses hybrid clocks and a max offset (500 ms by default), and lets a reader restart above values in its uncertainty window; parallel commits make a commit one consensus round. It's serializable, but not strictly.
Aurora DSQL is optimistic snapshot isolation with one check at commit, error 40001 on a clash, and limits of 3,000 rows, 10 MiB and 5 minutes.

The limit: every design pays a consensus round per write and some coordination per transaction, and distributed SQL doesn't mean serializable. For data that fits on one PostgreSQL server, that server is still cheaper; check the isolation level before you move.
closing:
We started with a friend's app that didn't yet show the money you sent. Trusting clocks that disagree is one way a database on many machines gets that gap. An oracle avoids it with one server, Spanner waits out the clock's error, and CockroachDB makes the reader check.

Next time you move money between two of your own accounts, open the second one at once. Is the money there? Which of this lesson's designs could promise it always is?

That ends Consistency and consensus, and Part III, Data across machines. Part IV, Moving and deriving data, opens with Messaging and logs. Next, we'll stop calling every program directly, and ask what should hold a message while the program that needs it is away.

quiz.q: A transfer has written intents on two ranges, and its transaction record says COMMITTED, but the intent on the second range hasn't been tidied up yet. A reader whose timestamp is above the commit timestamp reaches that intent. What must it do?
options: Skip it and read the older committed version
Find out the transaction's outcome (wait for, or look up, its record), and then read the committed value
Abort, because intents mean the data is corrupt
Read the intent's value without checking anything
quiz.why: The intent belongs to a committed transaction whose timestamp is below the reader's, so the reader must see it. Skipping it, the first option, would show the first range's half of the transfer and not this one's: a fractured read. The transaction record is the single place that decides, which is why a reader checks it, or waits, instead of guessing from the intent. Reading the intent blindly fails the other way: the intent of a transaction that later aborts must never be seen.

quiz.q: Spanner's TrueTime reports ε = 4 ms, and copying the commit record through Paxos takes 9 ms. Roughly how much does commit wait add to a write, and why?
options: About 8 ms on top of the 9 ms, since 2ε is always added
Nothing at all, because TrueTime uses atomic clocks
Little or none of the 2ε = 8 ms, because the wait runs while the commit record is copied; the paper measured about 5 ms of commit wait, with ε peaking at 7 ms
Exactly ε = 4 ms
quiz.why: The wait lasts until TrueTime's earliest passes the timestamp, about 2ε after it was picked, and Spanner runs it while Paxos copies the commit record. So only the part longer than the copying shows. The first option forgets that overlap. Atomic clocks make ε small; they don't make it zero, and the rule still waits.

quiz.q: CockroachDB runs with the default 500 ms max offset. A dashboard query reads a row that another node updated 200 ms ago, by that node's clock. What can happen?
options: The value is inside the read's uncertainty interval, so the read moves its timestamp above it, and may restart
Nothing: the value is 200 ms old, so it's clearly in the past
The query blocks for 500 ms of commit wait
The node shuts itself down for clock skew
quiz.why: Any value with a timestamp between the read's timestamp and 500 ms above it may have committed before the read began, on a node with a faster clock, so the read can't place it. CockroachDB moves the read's timestamp up, and carries on if its earlier reads still hold, or restarts. The second option trusts the other node's clock, which is exactly what the max offset refuses to do. There's no commit wait, and a node stops itself only when its own clock is off by 80% of the max offset from most others.

quiz.q: From Consistency models: what a read may return. CockroachDB defaults to SERIALIZABLE; Spanner promises external consistency. What does Spanner promise that plain serializability doesn't?
options: That transactions never abort
That the order of transactions agrees with real time: a transaction that starts after another has committed sees its effects (strict serializability)
That reads never block
That write skew is impossible
quiz.why: Serializability only says the result equals some one-at-a-time order, which may put a later transaction first, so a read can be stale. External consistency adds real-time order, which is strict serializability. Both rule out write skew, so the last option doesn't tell them apart, and neither promises no aborts or no blocking.

quiz.q: A team moves its fee job to Aurora DSQL. Two transactions each read a shop's two fee limits and lower one of them, so that the sum stays above a floor. Both commit, and the sum ends below the floor. Why?
options: DSQL lost one of the writes
The adjudicator failed

DSQL runs snapshot isolation only: the transactions wrote different rows, so neither clashes at commit, and write skew is allowed. Make them clash (both write one shared row), or read the rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
The 3,000-row limit was exceeded
quiz.why: Snapshot isolation checks only clashes between writes. Each transaction read both limits and wrote a different one, so the adjudicator saw no overlap: the write skew of the Transactions track. Nothing was lost and nothing failed, which rules out the first two options. In DSQL, `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` is checked as a write, so reading both limits that way makes the second commit fail with 40001 instead.

flashcards.front: Which four earlier ideas does a distributed SQL database stack?
flashcards.back: Key ranges on many machines, a consensus group per range, two-phase commit across ranges (intents plus a replicated transaction record), and versioned rows read at commit timestamps.

flashcards.front: What is a timestamp oracle, and what does it cost?
flashcards.back: One server (Percolator, TiDB's Placement Driver) that hands out increasing timestamps, so they follow real time. Every transaction makes a round trip to that one leader.
An interval [earliest, latest] that contains the true time. ε is half its width: about 1 to 7 ms in the 2012 paper.
Spanner commits at TT.now().latest and tells no one until TT.now().earliest has passed that timestamp: about 2ε, overlapped with Paxos.
From a read's timestamp up to that timestamp plus the max offset (500 ms by default). A value inside it can't be placed, so the read moves above it or restarts.

flashcards.front: What isolation does Aurora DSQL offer?
flashcards.back: Snapshot isolation only (PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ), optimistic, checked at commit: a clash returns 40001 with OC000.

terms.plain: A SQL database whose tables are split into ranges on many machines, with transactions that span them.
A provisional value a transaction writes before it commits. It also acts as a lock.
One server that hands out timestamps that only go up, to every transaction.
Transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, in the order they really happened. Spanner calls it external consistency.
Spanner's clock: it returns an interval [earliest, latest] that is guaranteed to contain the true time.
Holding back a commit's announcement until its timestamp is surely in the past on every clock.
The timestamps right above a read's own that may belong to writes made before the read began.
CockroachDB's commit that marks the transaction record STAGING while the intents are copied, so a commit takes one consensus round.

explain_back.prompt: Explain why a distributed SQL database can't stamp each commit with the local clock of the server that runs it, and two ways real systems avoid the problem.
explain_back.answer: A snapshot read returns everything committed at or below its timestamp. If each server uses its own clock and the clocks disagree, a payment committed on a server whose clock runs fast can carry a higher timestamp than a report started later on a server whose clock runs slow. The report then misses a payment that was already confirmed: a stale read, even though each transaction was all-or-nothing. Spanner avoids it with TrueTime, which reports an interval that surely contains the true time. It commits at the top of the interval and waits, about twice the clock error, until the bottom has passed that timestamp before telling anyone, so every later transaction gets a higher timestamp. CockroachDB avoids it without special clocks. It promises a maximum offset between clocks, shuts down nodes that exceed it, and makes a reader that meets a value right above its own timestamp, within that offset, move its timestamp up or restart. A third way is a single timestamp oracle, as in TiDB, at the price of a round trip to one server.

deeper.body:
**More on the oracles.** TiDB's timestamp is 64 bits: 46 bits of physical milliseconds and an 18-bit counter. Its default transaction mode is pessimistic, with locks taken as rows are written, and its REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation under a MySQL name, so it allows write skew. FoundationDB's authors say that a transaction hitting the five-second limit usually means a client is doing its reads one at a time.

**Percolator's cleanup.** Percolator commits by rewriting one primary lock, and the other locks point at it. A reader that finds a lock left by a crashed client checks the primary and rolls the transaction forward or back. That lazy cleanup could delay commits by tens of seconds: fine for building a search index, which was its job, and far too slow for a payment.

**Weaker levels in CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.** CockroachDB also offers READ COMMITTED, with a fresh snapshot per statement and no restarts, at the price of lost updates and write skew. YugabyteDB can take its clock bound from AWS's ClockBound daemon instead of a fixed 500 ms; on AWS that bound is typically well under a millisecond.

**Deterministic databases.** Calvin (2012) agrees on the order of whole transactions first, through a replicated log, and then every replica runs them in that order with no two-phase commit at all. The price is declaring a transaction's reads and writes up front. FaunaDB built on the idea, and Cassandra 6.0's Accord, still alpha, orders multi-partition transactions without a leader.

**Better clocks for everyone.** AWS's Time Sync Service gives EC2 instances an error bound under 100 µs over NTP and under 40 µs through the Nitro hardware clock, and its ClockBound daemon reports [earliest, latest] like TrueTime. As cloud clocks improve, commit wait and uncertainty windows shrink toward the cost of a consensus round, and the designs in this lesson converge.

**Reading further.** Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, covers distributed transactions in chapter 8, and timestamps, linearizable ID generators and consensus in chapter 10.
